description: Students from Sri Lanka building with open space data.
summary:
NASA EIC (Earth Information Centre) Data is almost always visual. 

JODI makes the planet's VISUAL data usable without sight, by keyboard, touch, voice or a screen reader. 

Global data, made accessible to 2.2 Billions of visually impaired community. 

Here's how it works:
You can move a small listening window over a real 3D globe.
The data inside and around it plays as a looping soundscape. 

Special features :
- Auditory assistant JODI supports even a completely non-visual person to navigate without an issue. 
- You can access spatial and temporal data both at once in one tool!
- You have access to customize the experience in so many ways!
- Beyond music, what you listen to is the raw sounds of the Earth.
details:
What it does

JODI: Feel the Earth is an "Earth Information Jukebox". A small listening window (2° to 30° wide) sits on a real Blue Marble globe. Whatever NASA data lies under and around the window plays as a 4-bar musical loop. Glide the window across the Indian Ocean and you hear warm water as a full, dark cello section. Cross into a lightning hotspot and glockenspiel strikes and rain fill the mix. Step through time by day or month and hear seasons change.

How it works: sonification

  1. Data: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio / Earth Information Center visualisations (sea surface temperature, ISS lightning, Black Marble night lights and their change from 2012 to 2023), and five NASA GIBS monthly layers (AIRS CO₂ and air temperature, MERRA-2 precipitation and aerosol optical depth, MODIS NDVI vegetation). The pipeline reads colours back to numbers using each product's colour bar or GIBS colour map, then stores 1° global grids that work offline.
    • Value: rhythm density, loudness and chord tone
    • Gradient: timbre, from pure tone to bright and metallic
    • Roughness: articulation, from long soft notes to short plucked ones
    • Danger line: a semitone clash
    • Bearing and distance: 3D direction
  2. Harmony: 72 bpm, key of D, one chord per bar. Every point sings a tone of the current chord, so overlapping data forms chords, not noise. The most severe active layer picks the mood (calm, uneasy, severe). In the severe mood, tremolo strings and a timpani heartbeat enter.

Figure 1. Sonification pipeline. NASA imagery (SVS, GIBS) is turned back into numbers through each product's colour bar, giving a 1° value grid. The listening window (orange) and the Earth-anchored points around it are sampled. Each point's five features (value, gradient, roughness, danger line, bearing and distance) each drive one sound dimension. Recorded instruments play the result in key and on the beat, and an HRTF places it in 3D for headphones.

Immersive surround sound

Every data point is placed around the listener with an HRTF panner: north ahead, east on the right, south behind. Nearer points are louder and brighter. Moving never changes pitch, only direction and distance, so any change in pitch or timbre is always the data. Gliding from the Arabian Sea across India to the Bay of Bengal, the warm sea moves from the left ear to the right. Peak and valley beacons (keys B and V) ping from the direction of the highest and lowest values nearby and speed up as you approach.

Figure 2. Immersive surround sound. Left: top-down view of the listener inside the listening window (orange). Each data point sounds from its true bearing θ (north ahead, east on the right). Gain and brightness fall with distance r, and pitch never depends on θ or r. Right: stereo balance measured from the app's audio output as the window glides east across India. The warm Arabian Sea starts in the left ear, and the balance moves toward the right as the Bay of Bengal comes into range.

Navigation without looking

  • Keyboard: arrows glide, + / − resize, number keys toggle layers, comma / full stop step time, W "where am I?", H "what am I hearing?", T guided listening tour.
  • Touch and mouse: drag spins the globe under a fixed window; tap jumps.
  • Earcons and haptic pulses: two wooden ticks at borders, a wave wash at coasts, a singing bowl at the equator, a small bell at the tropics, a whoosh that follows speed, and silent haptic ticks across contour steps.
  • Screen reader: everything is mirrored to an aria-live region.
  • JODI: a voice assistant. Say "Hey Jodi" or hold J. JODI is an AI agent that uses the same tools as the user (go to a place, switch layers, change the date, find peaks). Example: "Take me to Peru and play lightning" flies the window there and replies "There you go, we're over Peru with the lightning layer humming along."

Figure 3. Navigation loop. Keyboard, touch, voice and screen reader all control one listening window. Voice requests go through JODI, an AI agent that uses the same tools as the user. Every change comes back to the listener through spatial sonification, through earcons and haptic pulses, and through spoken answers, so the listener stays oriented without sight.

Benefits and impact

Blind and low-vision people, people whose eyes are busy elsewhere, and classrooms can explore real NASA Earth data by ear. Sound also shows patterns that colour maps hide: edges, fronts and patchiness become timbre and rhythm.

Built with

React and TypeScript, MapLibre GL globe, Tone.js with recorded instruments (VSCO 2 Community Edition, CC0), Web Audio HRTF panning, a Python data pipeline (NumPy, Pillow), PWA with offline cache, Capacitor Android app, Groq-hosted LLM for JODI's reasoning, Fish Audio for JODI's voice.

What's next

Blindfold listening tests with blind and low-vision users, more devices, finer data grids and classroom tours.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility first: everything works without sight by keyboard, touch, voice and screen reader, with haptics as a second channel.
  • Honest mapping: every sound traces to a data value, documented in a public mapping table. When there is no data, the layer is silent; nothing stands in for it.
  • Listenability: all layers share one key and chord progression, so stacking up to four layers stays musical. Each instrument has its own register and frequency band.
  • Movement vs. data: in early testing, pitch changes while moving were hard to tell apart from data changes. Movement now only changes direction and distance, and pitch belongs to the data.
  • Data fidelity: values are recovered from NASA colour maps, and every layer's source, time range and grid are documented, including known source issues.
  • Offline and low-bandwidth use: the app installs as a PWA and caches its data and audio.
  • Licensing: only public-domain NASA data and openly licensed (CC0 / CC BY) audio, credited per file.
  • Security: AI service keys stay on our server, never in the browser.
